lesson.title: Chasing the Tail: Formalizing Limits at Infinity
lesson.summary: A limit at infinity captures precisely what value, if any, a function approaches as its input grows without bound, giving the rigorous definition behind every horizontal asymptote calculation.
lesson.body:
Earlier sections used phrases like as x approaches infinity somewhat informally when describing horizontal asymptotes. A limit at infinity makes that idea precise. The statement that the limit of f(x) as x approaches infinity equals L means that for every degree of closeness you might demand between f(x) and L, no matter how strict, you can always find a cutoff value M such that once x is larger than M, f(x) is guaranteed to be that close to L. A parallel definition covers x approaching negative infinity, using a cutoff on the negative side instead.

This is precisely the rigorous version of the horizontal asymptote idea: the line y = L is a horizontal asymptote of f exactly when the limit of f(x) as x approaches positive infinity equals L, or the limit as x approaches negative infinity equals L. So a limit at infinity is the computational tool, and a horizontal asymptote is its graphical picture, two views of the same underlying fact.

The main technique for evaluating a limit at infinity of a rational expression is to divide every term, in both numerator and denominator, by the highest power of x appearing anywhere in the denominator, then use the fact that 1/x raised to any positive integer power approaches 0 as x approaches infinity. This single technique quietly reproduces every case of the degree-comparison rule from the horizontal asymptote discussion, since dividing by the highest power in the denominator automatically sends any lower-degree numerator term to 0 while leaving a finite ratio when the degrees match.

For a worked example, compute the limit of (3x^2 - x)/(5x^2 + 2) as x approaches infinity. Dividing every term by x^2, the highest power present, gives (3 - 1/x)/(5 + 2/x^2). As x approaches infinity, 1/x approaches 0 and 2/x^2 approaches 0, so the expression approaches (3 - 0)/(5 + 0) = 3/5. So the limit of (3x^2 - x)/(5x^2 + 2) as x approaches infinity is 3/5.

A numerical check confirms this: at x = 1000, the numerator is 3,000,000 - 1000 = 2,999,000 and the denominator is 5,000,000 + 2 = 5,000,002, giving a ratio of approximately 0.5998, very close to 3/5 = 0.6. As x approaches negative infinity, the same limit of 3/5 results, since the dominant terms are even powers of x; checking at x = -1000 gives numerator 3,000,000 + 1000 = 3,001,000 and the same denominator 5,000,002, for a ratio near 0.6002, again close to 0.6.

This divide-by-the-highest-power technique is exactly the same shortcut used for the degree-comparison rule in the horizontal asymptote discussion, now stated as a general method rather than a memorized case list. It applies just as well to expressions with square roots or several variable terms mixed together, as long as you divide by the fastest-growing piece in the denominator. It will be reused, and extended beyond rational functions, when describing the broader end behavior of a function, the topic taken up next.
